stories.title: a room is a place
stories.moment: Callum sent a link to the scheduler redesign. I wrote back "this is right." Two days later he sent the timeline view. I asked for the room block to read as a wall, not a card. He tried solid fills. I said yes. Then he stopped and wrote a paragraph about why the old design felt wrong: "a room is a place and an appointment is a promise and we were treating both as boxes." A place is persistent, has a location, can be empty. A promise is conditional, temporary, belongs to people. So the room should be a column that exists whether anything is scheduled or not. I told him it was the smartest thing anyone had said about this product.
stories.why_it_matters: The best design insight arrived after the fix was already approved.

stories.title: the invoice that took a month
stories.moment: Callum asked if invoices still went to Dane's email. I told him accounting@thicket.vet, he resent. Eight days later he asked if it went through, Stripe usually hits by now. I didn't answer. Five days after that I said the PO number didn't match our system, could he resend with the date-based format. He said he'd just copied it from last month's, did it change. Four days later I admitted Dane changed the format in QuickBooks and didn't tell anyone including me. He resent. Eleven days after that he wrote again: "really sorry to chase again but it's been a month, rent is tomorrow and i'm short." It had been sitting in approvals. Dane didn't realize it needed two signatures now.
stories.why_it_matters: Every reply arrived days late and moved the problem to a new broken thing.

stories.title: Failure stories are more useful than success stories
stories.moment: Marguerite signed the investment documents and sent them back the same morning, then offered three things. The third was an introduction to two people who had tried to sell software into independent practices and shut down. I told her that was "the single most useful offer anyone has made me this year," which was true but probably sounded like I was overselling my gratitude. She wrote back 16 words: "'One is real and two are polite' is a better summary than most seed decks manage." No reassurance that I hadn't been rude, no clarification of which pilot she meant. Just that line, and then the introductions went out six days later exactly as promised.
stories.why_it_matters: The correction arrived without any cushioning around it.

stories.title: I didn't answer the question
stories.moment: Marguerite asked three questions about the pilots in mid-May. I answered the first two in detail: the scheduling rewrite took eleven days, Rosalind was logging in daily, the polite pilots had gone quiet. Then I sent the May update two weeks later and she replied that the logins observation was good. A week after that she wrote back on the original thread: "I do not think you answered the third question." She was right. The question had been whether anyone was paying me yet, and I had written around it for two paragraphs without saying no. When I finally did say no, two days later, I added that I'd been reluctant to talk pricing while the product was breaking. She waited thirteen days, then replied that I had now told her twice I'd have an answer after a conversation I hadn't scheduled yet.
stories.why_it_matters: Every deflection gets named, and nothing gets named twice.

stories.title: Drainage Characteristic Rather Than Systemic Issue
stories.moment: Ezra sent a three-point memo explaining that standing water in the bathroom was not a plumbing problem but a feature of the building's original construction, where the floor drain sat at a lower grade than the supply line. He followed up the next day to report that the water level had decreased, "which confirms my assessment." The day after that he sent a final note saying the floor was now dry and would "resolve naturally within 24 to 48 hours" if it happened again. I sent one line back on the first day and nothing after that.
stories.why_it_matters: The explanation arrived in triplicate before anyone asked for it.

stories.title: Not Flooding, Water Accumulation Due to Usage Patterns
stories.moment: When the bathroom flooded again a month later, Ezra blamed it on excessive water usage at the sinks and improper paper towel disposal. I asked whether the floor was flooding because we were washing our hands too enthusiastically. He wrote back the next morning to clarify: not "flooding," but "water accumulation due to usage patterns. The distinction is important from a liability perspective." He explained that the faucet pressure was commercial-grade and referenced section 4.2 of the Tenant Guidelines. I wrote back that we would be more careful. Two days later he thanked me for my cooperation and noted that he had "documented this exchange and the resolution" in case we needed to revisit the facilities clause in the lease.
stories.why_it_matters: The correction of a single word generated more text than the original complaint.

stories.title: A Simple Agreed or Confirmed Will Suffice
stories.moment: After another incident Ezra sent a five-point outline of tenant responsibilities for the shared bathroom. I replied "Acknowledged." The next day he wrote back to say that for record-keeping purposes he would need explicit confirmation that we agreed to observe points one through five, and that "a simple 'agreed' or 'confirmed' will suffice." I sent back the word "confirmed" in lowercase with no punctuation. He filed it and said he would refer back to the exchange and the responsibilities as outlined on June 15 should any future incidents occur.
stories.why_it_matters: Every exchange ends with him documenting that the exchange has ended.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: He sent a five-point list of tenant responsibilities for the shared bathroom on June 15, then asked me to confirm in writing that we agree to them. I wrote 'confirmed' on June 17.

She wasn't looking but was curious, and insisted I answer two questions in writing before a call, "because I think written answers are more honest than spoken ones." One asked how I spent my engineering time last week. I gave her the breakdown: eleven hours on scheduling, six on a stalled migration, four on a billing question I'd decided not to answer, and nine hours I could not account for. She wrote back three days later that the nine unaccounted hours was "the most credible thing anyone has told me about a startup in a while."

I told her it gets resolved by arguing, and that we hadn't had the real argument yet, only the friendly version twice. I wrote that Dane owns what we sell, I own what we build, "and every real decision lives exactly on that line." I added that it works now with three customers because the answer is usually obvious, but I didn't think it would survive twenty customers without one of us having veto power. She replied that this was a good answer and confirmed the call. The structural question never came up again.

stories.title: The venmo that never came
stories.moment: I said yes to the radio and that I'd send money by the end of the week. Six days later Wendy wrote back: she hadn't gotten it, and she wasn't chasing me for it, but Rahul thought she'd forgotten to ask. The phrasing did all the work. Not 'you forgot,' not 'can you send it,' just the arrangement of whose problem this had become in someone else's head. I never sent it and she never asked again.
stories.why_it_matters: The thing that doesn't get mentioned twice is the thing someone has stopped expecting.

stories.title: Twenty days later she asked whether to set a place for me at all
stories.moment: Wendy asked on June 2nd whether I could come the Friday before the party to help with the cake, the chairs, and the tent. She wrote that it would be really nice to not do it by herself. I wrote back three days later that I'd look at the calendar that week and get back to her. I did not get back to her. Twenty days later she wrote again. She knew I was busy, she said, not in a pointed way. The tent people needed a final count by Monday. "I'd just like to know if I should set a place for you." The question was whether I was coming to the party at all.
stories.why_it_matters: Promising to check the calendar is a way of saying no while appearing to say maybe.

hero_line: Ten messages across eight weeks, and I've written first after every silence.

timeline.title: Billing is a trapdoor, he said

timeline.evidence: Billing is a trapdoor. Don't.

timeline.evidence: Neither of those is a product problem.

timeline.evidence: Fair enough. Good luck with it.

timeline.evidence: Otherwise you're choosing between your rule and payroll, and payroll wins every time.

timeline.title: The twenty-implementation cap, written down
timeline.description: I argued twenty implementations could produce a self-installing product, and he told me to make the rule visible to Dane.
timeline.evidence: Rules you keep in your own head aren't rules.

stories.title: Billing is a trapdoor
stories.moment: I asked whether to build billing, since two of three customers had requested it and Dane thought it would close the seed round. Theo sent back one line: "That's a features list, not a product." He pointed out that only one of the three customers was actually using what we'd already built, and asked why nobody had checked on that yet. I pushed back hard—I did know why the other two weren't using it, and neither reason was a product problem. He replied the next morning with six words: "Fair enough. Good luck with it." Twenty-three days later I cut billing from the roadmap and admitted the front desk manager had been a product problem all along. I'd built for her replacement without noticing I was making that choice.
stories.why_it_matters: The concession came three weeks later by email, not on the call where he was right.

stories.title: Twenty implementations, then stop
stories.moment: I wrote to him about the services question—every vertical software company in a low-margin industry eventually gets asked to do implementations, and I was wondering whether we should commit to a hard stop after some fixed number. He replied that it's "the thing everybody says at ten," and that the stop only holds if replacement revenue already exists before you stop. I argued back: if twenty implementations produce a product that installs itself, the replacement revenue isn't a bet, it's the output. The rule holds because by the time we get to twenty we don't want the work anymore. He sent back "That's a better argument than the one I was expecting," then told me to write the number down somewhere Dane could see it. "Rules you keep in your own head aren't rules."
stories.why_it_matters: Every argument ends with one of us conceding, but never the same person twice.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: I made the case for capping implementation services at twenty instead of ten, and he said it was a better argument than he expected. He told me to write the cap down where Dane can see it.
open_threads: I never told him whether I actually wrote the twenty-implementation cap down, or where I put it.
He asked me to tell him how Thursday went—the one after the room-based scheduling decision—and I never did.
three_talking_points: Ask whether he still thinks the cap breaks at ten, now that I've written it down.
Tell him what happened with the front desk manager and whether she actually used the thing before October.
Ask whether he's seen the services-to-product pattern break in a way that wasn't just a founder lying to themselves about the stop date.

stories.title: per-seat pricing is fear written down
stories.moment: Josiah sent unsolicited notes on the pricing page, saying per-seat turns the front desk into a cost center and clinics will just share a login. I wrote back at 11pm and admitted we went per-seat because it was "the thing I understood how to build, which is a bad reason that I have been calling a pricing strategy for four months." The FAQ disclaimer about features coming soon was staying on the page out of fear, nothing else. He'd caught me pricing the product around what I knew how to implement instead of what the customer actually needed, and I knew it the second I read it.
stories.why_it_matters: The pricing model was built backward from implementation comfort, not customer value.

stories.title: I said yes and then went silent
stories.moment: Josiah asked for an intro to Marguerite Vance, who led my round. I said I'd think about the framing "so it actually lands" and asked for a few days. Twenty-seven days later he sent a second nudge, offering to draft the blurb himself to make it a "two-minute thing instead of a twenty-minute thing." I never answered. Twenty-one days after that he wrote one last time: "I'd just rather know than keep wondering whether my email went to spam." The intro never happened. He stopped asking.
stories.why_it_matters: Saying yes and disappearing is worse than saying no in the first place.

stories.title: hire for taste, budget the teaching cost
stories.when: the week after the pricing conversation
stories.moment: I asked whether domain background mattered for a first engineering hire. The candidate I wanted had no healthcare experience; the two who did were "both fine and neither is her." Josiah said he'd cared about domain and been wrong—the domain hire plateaued after ten weeks because he kept building what the industry already did, while the one who knew nothing "asked why four times a day and two of those questions were good. One of them changed the product." Then the real answer: "it only worked because I was there to answer the why questions." I realized the right question was whether I had the hours to be her domain for two months, and I didn't love my answer.
stories.why_it_matters: The constraint wasn't the candidate's background, it was whether I could afford to teach someone worth teaching.

forgotten.summary: I promised Josiah I would introduce him to Marguerite Vance (who led my funding round) after thinking about the right framing. He followed up twice (May 6 and May 27) and I never sent the intro or responded.
forgotten.suggested_action: Send Josiah a direct response: either make the intro to Marguerite with specific framing, or explain honestly why I can't.

stories.title: the room that was two rooms
stories.moment: Beatriz set up all five rooms in the system after we walked through the clinic. Then she sent a second email the same day: Exam 2 and Exam 3 were actually one room with a curtain down the middle. They tracked them separately because they could double-book for exams, but if one side had surgery prep they had to block both. She flagged it "before someone books a neuter on one side and a puppy wellness check on the other." I hadn't asked about edge cases. She caught it on her own, five days before it would have broken in production.
stories.why_it_matters: The failure mode arrived in an email, not in a customer complaint.

stories.title: manual block-both toggle for now
stories.moment: I wrote back that it "matters a lot" and that I was "going to need to think about how to model that without making the interface horrible." The interim fix was a manual toggle. No argument about whether the curtain setup was reasonable, no request to change their workflow. She had described the constraint; I accepted that the software had to bend around it. The phrase I used was "for now," which meant I knew it was a workaround and she knew I knew.
stories.why_it_matters: The product adjusted to the clinic, not the other way around.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: I came in on May 9th to set up room assignments. She flagged that Exam 2 and Exam 3 are one room with a curtain, and they double-book for exams but block both sides for surgery prep.
